Content:
Any two circles are similar because any circle can be mapped to any other circle using a combination of similarity transformations.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the circles [MATH: \mathcal C] and [MATH: \mathcal C'] centered at [MATH: O] and with radii [MATH: 2] and [MATH: 4,] respectively.

We can double the radius of [MATH: \mathcal{C}] so that it has the same radius as [MATH: \mathcal{C}'.] To do this, we use a dilation with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: 2.]

items.title: Determining a Dilation That Maps One Circle Onto Another

sections.normalized_html: What transformation maps the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C}] with center at the origin and radius [MATH: 2] onto the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C'}] with center at the origin and radius [MATH: 8?]
sections.readable_text: What transformation maps the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C}] with center at the origin and radius [MATH: 2] onto the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C'}] with center at the origin and radius [MATH: 8?]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that both circles have center [MATH: O.] So, mapping [MATH: \mathcal{C}] onto [MATH: \mathcal{C'}] can be done using only a dilation.

The radius of [MATH: \mathcal C] is [MATH: r_1 = 2] units, and the radius of [MATH: \mathcal C'] is [MATH: r_2 = 8] units. Therefore, the required dilation has a scale factor of

[MATH: k = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4.]

Therefore, to map the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C}] onto the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C'},] we apply a dilation with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: 4.]

items.title: Describing a Similarity Transformation Using Function Composition

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following functions:

[MATH: f(x,y)=(x+p,y+q), \qquad g(x,y)=(kx,ky)]

The function [MATH: f(x,y)] is applied to [MATH: \mathcal C,] and then [MATH: g(x,y)] is applied to the result. The image of [MATH: \mathcal C] under this sequence of transformations is [MATH: \mathcal C'.] What is [MATH: p+q+k?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/e85c0a91c988c80464a3d2c393c84c1a]

Consider the following functions:

[MATH: f(x,y)=(x+p,y+q), \qquad g(x,y)=(kx,ky)]

The function [MATH: f(x,y)] is applied to [MATH: \mathcal C,] and then [MATH: g(x,y)] is applied to the result. The image of [MATH: \mathcal C] under this sequence of transformations is [MATH: \mathcal C'.] What is [MATH: p+q+k?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we note the following:

  • the function [MATH: f(x,y) = (x+p,y+q)] represents a translation of [MATH: p] units right and [MATH: q] units up, and

  • the function [MATH: g(x,y) = (kx,ky)] is a dilation of scale factor [MATH: k.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Any two circles are similar because any circle can be mapped to any other circle using a combination of similarity transformations.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the circles [MATH: \mathcal C] and [MATH: \mathcal C'] centered at [MATH: O] and with radii [MATH: 2] and [MATH: 4,] respectively.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e475a6345370e23d729e442b777f151f]

Content:
We can double the radius of [MATH: \mathcal{C}] so that it has the same radius as [MATH: \mathcal{C}'.] To do this, we use a dilation with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: 2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/497816b0fcb09f9c627bc5179f74e04c]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathcal C] is mapped to [MATH: \mathcal C'] under this transformation, the two circles are similar.

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining a Dilation That Maps One Circle Onto Another

Example Prompt:
What transformation maps the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C}] with center at the origin and radius [MATH: 2] onto the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C'}] with center at the origin and radius [MATH: 8?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that both circles have center [MATH: O.] So, mapping [MATH: \mathcal{C}] onto [MATH: \mathcal{C'}] can be done using only a dilation.

The radius of [MATH: \mathcal C] is [MATH: r_1 = 2] units, and the radius of [MATH: \mathcal C'] is [MATH: r_2 = 8] units. Therefore, the required dilation has a scale factor of

[MATH: k = \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4.]

Therefore, to map the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C}] onto the circle [MATH: \mathcal{C'},] we apply a dilation with center [MATH: O] and scale factor [MATH: 4.]
